title: Broca, Wernicke, and language areas
text:
CHAPTER 3. LOCALIZING FUNCTION
SECTION 3.2. BROCA, WERNICKE, AND LANGUAGE AREAS

A patient called Tan

In April 1861, a 51-year-old man named Louis Victor Leborgne was transferred to the surgical ward of the Bicetre hospital near Paris, where Paul Broca (1824 to 1880) was a surgeon. Leborgne had been a patient at Bicetre for many years. He had lost the ability to speak decades earlier; the usual account is that this happened around the age of 30. He could understand much of what was said to him, and he could communicate with gestures and changes of tone, but the only syllable he could reliably produce was "tan," which he often repeated twice ("tan tan"). Because of this, he was known in the hospital as "Tan." Over the years he had also developed paralysis on the right side of his body.

Leborgne died a few days after Broca examined him. Broca performed an autopsy and found a lesion on the surface of the left frontal lobe, centered in the posterior part of the third frontal convolution (the inferior frontal gyrus). The damage was extensive and had spread to surrounding areas, but Broca argued that the original lesion, the one that had caused the loss of speech, was in the frontal region. He presented the brain to the Society of Anthropology of Paris in April 1861 and published a detailed report later that year.

Leborgne's identity was obscure for a long time, and he was known in the literature only as Tan. Historical research published in the 2010s, especially by the Polish historian Cezary Domanski, identified him in archival records and described aspects of his life, such as his origins in Moret-sur-Loing and his work as a maker of lasts (forms used in making shoes). His brain is still preserved in Paris. In 2007, researchers led by Nina Dronkers used high-resolution MRI to scan the preserved brains of Leborgne and of a second Broca patient, Lelong, and found that the lesions extended deeper into the brain than Broca had described, involving underlying white matter and other structures. Since Broca chose not to dissect the brains, preserving them intact, he could not see the deep damage.

Why Broca's report mattered

Broca was not the first to suggest that language is localized in the frontal lobes. Gall had placed language there, and the French physician Jean-Baptiste Bouillaud had argued for decades, from clinical cases, that speech depends on the anterior lobes. Bouillaud's son-in-law, Ernest Aubertin, was actively debating localization at the Society of Anthropology at the time, and he had challenged opponents to find a case of loss of speech without frontal damage. Broca's patient provided a clear, carefully documented case at exactly the right moment, from a respected scientist, and his report was taken seriously in a way earlier claims had not been.

Broca followed up with more cases. Lelong, an 84-year-old man who had lost almost all speech after a stroke and could produce only a few words, was found at autopsy to have a lesion in roughly the same region. Over the next few years Broca accumulated additional cases. A striking pattern emerged: the lesions causing loss of speech were almost always on the left side.

In 1865 Broca published a paper stating that we speak with the left hemisphere. (The French physician Marc Dax had reportedly reached a similar conclusion earlier, in a manuscript from 1836 that was published by his son Gustave Dax in 1865, leading to a priority dispute.) This was a surprising claim. The two hemispheres of the brain look nearly symmetrical. That one side should be specialized for a function as important as language contradicted the expectation that paired organs do the same thing. The phenomenon is now called hemispheric lateralization, or cerebral dominance.

Broca called the disorder "aphemie" (aphemia); the term that stuck, "aphasia," was proposed by Armand Trousseau. The region of the left inferior frontal gyrus is now called Broca's area. In modern anatomical terms, it usually refers to the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus, which roughly correspond to Brodmann areas 44 and 45, though definitions vary.

What Broca's aphasia looks like

The syndrome now called Broca's aphasia (or expressive, nonfluent, or motor aphasia) typically includes:

- Slow, effortful, halting speech with reduced fluency.
- Short phrases with mostly content words (nouns and verbs) and few function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliary verbs) and inflections, a pattern called agrammatism, sometimes described as "telegraphic" speech.
- Relatively preserved comprehension of everyday speech, although comprehension of grammatically complex sentences can be impaired.
- Often, awareness of the deficit and frustration.
- Frequently, weakness of the right side of the body, because the nearby motor cortex is often also damaged.

It is important to note that the clinical syndrome called Broca's aphasia and damage limited to Broca's area are not the same thing. Damage restricted to Broca's area often produces milder or temporary deficits. The full syndrome usually requires larger lesions that include surrounding cortex and underlying white matter. This is consistent with the 2007 MRI findings on Broca's own patients.

Carl Wernicke and the comprehension area

In 1874, a young German physician named Carl Wernicke (1848 to 1905) published a monograph, Der aphasische Symptomencomplex ("The aphasic symptom complex"), when he was only about 26 years old. He described patients with a very different kind of language disorder. These patients spoke fluently, with normal rhythm and grammar-like structure, but their speech was often meaningless or full of errors, with wrong words or invented words (paraphasias and neologisms). Crucially, they had great difficulty understanding what others said. And they often seemed unaware of their own errors.

At autopsy, Wernicke found lesions in the posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus, near the auditory cortex. This region is now called Wernicke's area (roughly the posterior part of Brodmann area 22, though again definitions vary). The syndrome is called Wernicke's aphasia (or receptive, fluent, or sensory aphasia).

Wernicke's model: language as a network

Wernicke's most important contribution was not just identifying a second area. It was proposing a model of how language areas work together. He reasoned like an engineer:

- Wernicke's area, near the auditory cortex, stores the "sound images" of words, the auditory memory of what words sound like. It is needed to recognize spoken words and so to understand speech.
- Broca's area, near the motor cortex controlling the mouth and tongue, stores the "motor images" of words, the plans for articulating them. It is needed to produce speech.
- The two are connected by a pathway of nerve fibers. In speaking, the sound image in Wernicke's area guides the motor image in Broca's area. This explains why Wernicke's patients speak fluently but wrongly: Broca's area works, but it is no longer guided by correct sound images.

From this model, Wernicke made a prediction. If the connection between the two areas were cut, while both areas remained intact, the patient should be able to understand speech (Wernicke's area intact) and speak fluently (Broca's area intact), but should be unable to repeat what is heard accurately, and should make errors in spontaneous speech, because the sound images could not guide the motor images. This predicted syndrome is now called conduction aphasia, and patients with this pattern of deficits were indeed described. The connecting pathway was identified with the arcuate fasciculus, a bundle of white matter fibers arching around the Sylvian fissure.

Wernicke's model is a beautiful example of a theory that predicts a new phenomenon from the structure of a system. It is the first network model of a cognitive function: not a single center, but connected centers, where symptoms can arise from damage to a node or to a link.

The Wernicke-Lichtheim model and its descendants

In 1885 Ludwig Lichtheim extended Wernicke's scheme into a diagram with a third center for "concepts," connected to both Broca's and Wernicke's areas. The diagram, often called the Wernicke-Lichtheim "house" because of its shape, predicted several additional types of aphasia depending on which node or link was damaged, such as transcortical motor and transcortical sensory aphasia, in which repetition is preserved while other functions are lost. Diagrams like this were very popular among neurologists in the late nineteenth century, who were sometimes called "diagram makers." Some critics, including Henry Head in the early twentieth century, attacked them as too simplistic.

In the 1960s, the American neurologist Norman Geschwind revived and extended the connectionist approach, emphasizing "disconnection syndromes," in which deficits arise from damage to white matter pathways between areas. The resulting framework is often called the Wernicke-Geschwind model and appears in many textbooks.

The modern view of language in the brain

Modern research with brain imaging, intraoperative stimulation, and lesion-symptom mapping in large patient groups has shown that the classical model is incomplete. Some key revisions:

- Language involves a large network of regions, including much of the left frontal, temporal, and parietal cortex, and also subcortical structures and the right hemisphere for some aspects such as prosody (the melody of speech).
- Influential "dual stream" models, such as the one developed by Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel, propose a ventral stream in the temporal lobes for mapping sounds to meaning, and a dorsal stream linking temporal and parietal regions to frontal regions for mapping sounds to articulation. These are analogous to the dual streams in vision.
- There are at least two major white matter routes between frontal and temporal language regions, not just the arcuate fasciculus.
- Broca's area is involved in many functions besides speech production, including aspects of syntax, working memory, and possibly action understanding. Its exact role is still debated.
- Lateralization varies: the large majority of right-handed people have left-hemisphere language dominance, as do most left-handed people, but a significant minority of left-handers have right-hemisphere or bilateral language representation.

Despite these revisions, Broca's and Wernicke's work established clinical-pathological correlation as a method, demonstrated localization of a higher cognitive function, revealed hemispheric specialization, and introduced the idea that cognitive functions depend on networks of connected regions.

Bridge to AI: language models, modularity, and disconnection

The study of language in the brain has a fascinating relationship with modern AI.

Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained to predict the next word (or token) in text. They have no Broca's or Wernicke's area by design; their transformer architecture is uniform, with the same type of layer repeated many times. Yet researchers have looked inside these models for specialization and have found some: certain attention heads appear to track syntactic relations, such as which noun a verb agrees with; some components appear to handle specific tasks like copying or indirect object identification. Whether these resemble brain language areas is an open and interesting question.

There is also a converging line of research comparing language models with the brain directly. Several studies have found that the internal activations of language models can predict brain responses (measured with fMRI, MEG, or intracranial electrodes) to the same sentences, with models that are better at next-word prediction often predicting brain activity better. This has been interpreted by some as evidence that the brain's language network also performs something like prediction, though others caution that the correspondence may reflect shared statistics of language rather than shared mechanisms.

Neuroscientists such as Evelina Fedorenko have argued, from fMRI studies, that the human brain has a "language network" that is distinct from networks for general reasoning and for the "theory of mind" needed to understand other people. Patients with severe aphasia can still sometimes do arithmetic, play chess, or solve logic problems. This dissociation between language and thought has been used to argue that LLMs, which are trained on language, might be strong on formal linguistic competence but would need other mechanisms for robust reasoning and world knowledge. This "formal versus functional competence" distinction is a recent and active debate.

Finally, the disconnection idea from Wernicke has a parallel in network analysis. In both brains and artificial networks, a function can fail not because a component is damaged but because the connection between components is damaged. In deep networks, residual connections act like white matter highways that carry information past layers, and ablating them has very different effects from ablating layers. A good interpretability study, like a good neurology examination, considers both nodes and links.

Summary

- In 1861 Paul Broca reported that his patient Leborgne ("Tan"), who could understand speech but not produce it, had a lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus. Later cases led him to conclude in 1865 that language is usually lateralized to the left hemisphere.
- In 1874 Carl Wernicke described fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension, linked to damage in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus.
- Wernicke proposed a network model linking the two areas and predicted conduction aphasia from damage to the connecting fibers.
- Later work by Lichtheim, Geschwind, and modern researchers refined this into the view of language as a distributed, lateralized network with dorsal and ventral streams.
- Language models, interpretability studies, and brain-model comparisons are a new chapter in this old question of how language is organized.
